catalog_quote: The Chinantec languages are famous for their complex tone and stress systems. ... It is the stress (and its interactions with tone), however, that Chinantec is best known for. Syllables in most dialects of Chinantec can be stressless, can have a normal stress (called “controlled” in the literature), or can have what is known as “ballistic” stress. Controlled stress occurs on the final syllable of the word (although words are normally monosyllabic, so in practice this means stress occurs on the only syllable of the word), and is realized as vowel length and/or increased amplitude. ... At first glance, Ojitlán Chinantec appears to have a ballistic/controlled distinction (and in fact that was the analysis given in the original version of this paper). The primary cue was the extreme versions of the high and low tones; that is, a very high tone and a very low tone. ... However, Holsinger (19…
sweep_summary: One bibliography item only: Holsinger 1998 'Tone and Ballistic Stress in Ojitlán Chinantec', an unpublished University of Wisconsin-Madison ms. (Glottolog 303653) presented at the Jan 1998 LSA/SSILA meeting. Its full text is not online anywhere I could check (Crossref, archive.org, WorldCat, DDG/Bing: no hits; UW catalog 404); the only open text is the meeting abstract in the LSA 1998 handbook, already held by the project from the 9/16 check and now extracted to ( written there). The abstract is about the phonetic nature of ballistic stress (a [spread glottis] phonation type over a three-level tone system), not about stress placement, so the catalog's fixed: final syllable (in practice only-syllable) coding from Macaulay 1999 p.77 stands unchanged. It refines the catalog's tone_note: Macaulay 1999 (pp.77-78, fn 4; held by the project) reports Holsinger's ms. as showing no consistent ballistic correlates and five level tones, whereas Holsinger's own abstract keeps ballistic stress (as phonation) and a three-level system; the ms. (cited by Macaulay at pp.3-4) evidently developed after the abstract. Acquiring the ms. is medium priority (dedicated instrumental study of OC tone/stress, but unpublished; realistic route is to ask Monica Macaulay or David Holsinger). No new deciding source; Macaulay 1999 remains the catalog's the deciding source.

new_statements.quote: Instrumental phonetic analysis reveals numerous characteristics of OC that contradict many prior assumptions about this dialect. Among other things, the discovery of a 'very high' tone allows for a complete reanalysis of the tone and stress systems of OC. In light of this new data, OC can be described as having a more typical three-level system which then is affected by ballistic stress. Recent work by Silverman (1995), which suggests that 'ballistic stress' is better described as a phonation type than as a prosodic feature, is supported by the phonetic evidence at hand in OC. Acoustic cues such as postvocalic aspiration point to the association of ballistic stress with the feature [spread glottis], rather than features typically associated with prosody or stress.

new_statements.reading: First-hand instrumental statement on the nature of 'stress' in Ojitlán Chinantec: the ballistic/controlled distinction is a phonation-type ([spread glottis]) contrast overlaid on a three-level tone system, not a prosodic stress feature. It is silent on where word stress falls, so it cannot replace the catalog's positional rule (Macaulay 1999 p.77: controlled stress on the final, normally only, syllable of the word). It bears on the catalog's tone_note: Macaulay's summary of the same ms. ('no correlates of ballistic stress are consistently present'; five level tones) is stronger than what the abstract itself claims (OC 'affected by ballistic stress' as phonation; three-level system), so the tone_note should say that Macaulay's denial of a ballistic contrast is her reading of Holsinger's ms., while Holsinger's own abstract keeps ballistic stress as a phonation type.

tone_statements.citation: Smith, Dorothy & Paul Smith. [ca. 1960]. Chinantec Phonemes with Special Reference to the Tonal System. Unpublished manuscript, 5 pp., SIL Mexico Branch; SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 53237 (draft, posted 'as is'). PDF.
tone_statements.quote: Chinantec is a register-contour language of a type not previously described. Four phonemic registers are basic to the tonal system. The four registers are high (1), mid-high (2), mid-low (3), and low (4). Tones 1 and 4 may occur level or down-glided. ... Two types of phonemic glides must be distinguished. ... They are mid-high rising (2↗), mid-high falling (2↘), mid-low rising (3↗), and mid-low falling (3↘). ... On this basis we interpret all Type A glides as tonemic entities. ... All eight tonemes and Type B glides occur after stops.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 1.1 Tonemes, pp.1-2; last sentence sec. 1.22, p.3
tone_statements.summary: 4 level registers + 4 short Type A glides = 8 unit tonemes; Type B glides (1-3, 1-2, 2-3) = register sequences; 3+4 > 4 4 perturbation; every syllable (= morpheme) carries a tone; arrows retyped ↗↘.

tone_statements.citation: Smith, Paul. 1955. Ojitlán Chinantec Syllable Constituents. Unpublished manuscript dated May 1955, 10 pp., SIL Mexico Branch; SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 47474 (draft, posted 'as is'). PDF.
tone_statements.quote: 3.3 OC has four phonemic registers of tone. The following examples illustrate the four register contrasts: kǫ2 či1 one head, kǫ2 či2 one gruel, kǫ2 či3 one wind, kǫ2 e2či4 one good thing. Tope 3 is always phonetically level, within the limits of perception. Nonphonemic downglides occur on tones 1, 2, and 4 when these occur on vowels of open syllables under the following conditions ... Of the possible sequences of two tones which might occur on single vowels, the following six occur in the data: 12, 13, 14, 23, 32, 31.

tone_statements.summary: Four level registers 1 (high) to 4 (low); glides 12,13,14,23,32,31 analysed as two tones on one vowel; downglides and post-glide lowering nonphonemic. p.3: stress placement 'is independent of pitch'.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim on printed p.77 (sec. 2.3) of the Macaulay 1999 PDF we hold (scanned), exactly as located. (2) Deciding source: a 1999 14-pp working-paper phonology sketch, the sole phonological description of Ojitlán Chinantec in Glottolog 5.1 (Glottolog lists 2 descriptive works; the other is a 1957/1962 proto-Chinantec mimeo). No reference grammar, dissertation, JIPA illustration or later acoustic study of this variety was found; SIL Mexico holds only the 1955 vocabulario, whose front matter (downloaded via the Internet Archive, read) gives four tone registers and no stress statement; the CIESAS repository's Chinantec theses are on Quiotepec and Temixtlán. Holsinger's 1998 LSA abstract (downloaded) concerns the ballistic-stress/phonation question, not stress position. So the best available source is held and quoted. (3) Caveat that keeps this at 'adequate' rather than 'well-sourced':

sources.note: Record: 'A description and comparison of Chinantec phonology using data from 23 localities representing some 13 distinct variants with a view towards reconstructing the phonological system of Proto Chinantec.' The synchronic sketches and correspondence sets necessarily include each variety's tones (Chinantec reconstruction is largely tonal), so it should contain an Ojitlán tone inventory and its Proto-Chinantec sources; tone is not itemised in the record itself.
